title: One boat (Leviticus Rabbah 4:6)
hook: a man drills under his own seat in a boat, and the water drowns everyone
tomorrow: why does Hillel call a trip to the bathhouse a mitzvah?

segments.voice: Last week ended on a daring line: when you are My witnesses, I am God. You are my witnesses. God known through what people do. Which raises a question about what one person does.
screen: `YOU ARE MY WITNESSES.` → `WHAT ONE PERSON DOES.`

segments.voice: The boat is already out on the water when someone hears it: a scraping sound, steady, under the benches. Heads turn. One passenger has a drill, and he's boring a hole in the floor, right under his own seat. What are you doing? He barely looks up. What's it to you? I'm only drilling under my own place. The others look at the hole, then at the water, then at each other. Somebody reaches for a cup to bail.
screen: `A SCRAPING UNDER THE BENCHES.` → `A DRILL, UNDER HIS OWN SEAT.` → `WHAT'S IT TO YOU?`

segments.voice: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai tells this parable in Leviticus Rabbah, and the passengers' answer is the whole point: the water will come up and flood the boat for all of us. Notice what the man gets right. It really is his seat. The parable never argues about who owns the spot. It argues about water, and water doesn't read seat numbers. He isn't even trying to sink anyone. He just thinks the boat ends where his bench does. Right beside it, the midrash brings a second picture, from a sage named Hezekiah, on the verse "Israel is a scattered sheep." When one sheep is hurt in its head or a leg, its whole body feels it. So too, the midrash says, when one person in Israel does wrong, all of them feel it. In the midrash, the boat is the people of Israel, bound to each other. Some readers today hear it more widely too: a team, a family, a town, everyone on one small planet. Here's the line to repeat tonight: the drill is his, the seat is his, and the sea belongs to everybody. That cuts both ways. It means one person's harm doesn't stay private. It also means nobody in the boat is a stranger to the others, and patching a hole is everyone's business too.
screen: `THE WATER FLOODS US ALL.` · `HIS SEAT, EVERYONE'S WATER.` · `ONE SHEEP HURT, ALL FEEL IT.` · `NOBODY IN THE BOAT IS A STRANGER.` · then, large: `WE'RE IN ONE BOAT.`

segments.voice: Stand up and walk slowly for one minute: around the room, down a hall, out the door if you can. Every few steps, name one person your choices this week will touch, and let the list grow longer than you expected. Then sit for the rest of the bell with everyone who's in your boat.
screen: `A SLOW MINUTE'S WALK.` · `WHO'S IN YOUR BOAT?` · `LET THE LIST GROW.`

segments.voice: One boat: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's parable in Leviticus Rabbah. A hole drilled under one seat floods the boat for everyone in it.
Your line: we're in one boat. The seat may be yours, but the water is everyone's.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching expresses this as kol Yisrael arevim zeh ba-zeh, 'all Israel are responsible for one another' (Shevuot 39a), and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's boat parable is often told to explain it.
